body: Monday, March 17 2025 — Macro · Sectors · Flows · Crypto
Information available before 2025-03-17 00:00 UTC. Prices use completed prior sessions. Prepared retrospectively; later outcomes are excluded.

Macro Stance: The S&P 500 closed at 5,638.94 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14), down 7.79% over 20 sessions even after a 2.13% bounce in the latest session. The index has slipped into correction, and CNN put it bluntly: “Dow slides and S&P 500 closes in correction as Trump’s trade war escalates” [1]. The pressure is coming through the household. Consumer sentiment fell to its lowest since 2022 on tariff worries [2], and inflation expectations jumped [3]. The 25% tariffs on steel and aluminum imports took effect and Europe retaliated [4]. The data cut the other way: February CPI eased to 2.8%, below forecasts [5], and the wholesale price measure was flat [6]. Washington removed one risk as well, with the spending bill signed and the shutdown averted [7] [8]. The Fed decides on Wednesday, and the pre-meeting framing is simply what to expect [9]. JPMorgan’s economist puts the odds of a US recession at 40% [10]. The data support holding risk while the tariff shock works through household budgets.

Rates & Curve: At the prior close the Treasury par curve had the 2Y at 4.02%, the 10Y at 4.31% and the 30Y at 4.62%, with the 10Y−2Y spread at +29 bps (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-14). Over 20 observations the 2Y fell 29 bps from 4.31% and the 10Y fell 21 bps from 4.52%, so the spread widened by 8 bps. The curve is positively sloped, and the 20-observation move is bull steepening (both down, 2Y down more) (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-14). The market is paying for earlier easing, not for a sharper cycle. Equities are pricing something else: the Nasdaq 100 is down 10.56% over 20 sessions, and the VIX, at 21.77, is up 44.17% over the same span (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). The dollar index sits at 103.72 index points, down 3.35% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14), and Bloomberg reports Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling the currency’s decline a natural adjustment [11]. Lower front-end yields with a softer dollar is the mix that rescues long-duration assets, but only if volatility stops rising.

New / Most Important: The signal that matters is what the household squeeze does to demand. Reuters reported consumer confidence sinking on tariff fears as inflation expectations jumped [3], and CNBC put March’s reading at its lowest since 2022 [2]. Retailers are saying the same thing. Dollar General’s chief executive warned that consumers are cash-strapped and that 2025 will not be better [12], and Business Insider quotes her saying shoppers only have enough money for ‘basic essentials’ [13]. The Fed is the other half of the trade. Bloomberg reports markets expect two cuts this year, starting in September [14], which is why the front end has rallied while equities fell. If the Wednesday decision keeps that path, the bond rally can carry. If it pushes back, the steepening stalls and the high-beta growth names that have been hit hardest face another leg down.

Playbook ✓: Stay at neutral equity exposure and rotate inside it rather than adding beta. Keep duration on through the Wednesday decision: the 2Y has already fallen 29 bps over 20 observations, and long Treasuries (TLT) are up 1.68% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14), so the market leans that way. Buy quality on down days rather than chasing the 2.13% bounce, and keep a volatility hedge while the VIX sits well above its February reference of 15.10 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). The call changes in two directions. A VIX close back under 15.10 with the 2Y still falling would make the rally broad and justify adding cyclicals. A 10Y yield back above its February level of 4.52%, with tariff escalation in the headlines, would argue for cutting duration and staying defensive.

Macro Stance: Europe is the best-positioned large block for the coming weeks, and the reason is fiscal rather than monetary. Germany struck a historic debt deal and the euro rallied on it [15] [16]. The ECB has already cut its key rate to 2.5% on March 6 [17], and German inflation fell, which gives the ECB more room to ease further [18]. EUR/USD is at 1.0856, up 3.77% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). Reuters’ morning note framed the shift as “Europe, China shine as US exceptionalism fades” [19], and the New York Times reports that Trump’s moves are boosting stocks overseas [20]. The caveat is that the rally is in the home market, not in US listings, since the FT notes that US listings often fail to lift European valuations [21].

Credit & Inflation: Inflation risk is two-sided. Lagarde warned that trade and defence shocks could amplify euro zone inflation [22], and that higher defence spending could push prices up [23]. The ECB wage tracker still points to easing negotiated wages [24], which keeps the disinflation path intact. Growth is weaker at the edges: the UK economy shrank unexpectedly in January [25], and France’s borrowing costs are near a 14-year high before a Fitch review [26]. The Bundesbank chief warned that US tariffs could extend Germany’s recession [27], which is why the German package matters for the whole bloc. The market shows the split: the DAX is at 22,986.82, up 2.10% over 20 sessions, while the STOXX 600 is at 546.60, down 1.05% over the same span (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14).

New / Most Important: The signal that matters is the German fiscal turn, and its beneficiaries are wider than defence. Euronews framed it as “Beyond defence: Stocks set to gain from Germany’s economic revolution” [28], and DIW says the fiscal expansion would boost German GDP from 2026 [29]. EU ministers have also backed a proposal for a temporary exemption on defence spending in EU rules [30]. Defence is the headline. Construction, industrial capex and utilities are the quieter channel the fiscal plan reaches.

Playbook ✓: Buy German and broad euro-area cyclicals on pullbacks, keep a defence sleeve as the hedge, and avoid the autos that tariff headlines are hitting. A euro long against the dollar makes sense now that the US shutdown risk has passed [8]. The call changes in two ways. A fresh US tariff escalation on EU goods, such as the 200% tariff threat on EU alcohol [31], would move the block to neutral. An ECB pause read as a tightening bias would do the same, although the cut to 2.5% makes that unlikely in the near term.

Macro Stance: Beijing is talking about demand, and equity markets are listening. Beijing has said it will “vigorously boost consumption” [32], and the plan arrives as a 30-point toolbox [33]. The central bank said it will create “more tools” to shore up the economy [34]. The 5% growth target leaves most of the work to policy [35], and Fortune argues China has only one real way to hit it [36]. The official data are mixed rather than weak. The non-manufacturing PMI was 50.4 in February [37], but Bloomberg’s headline says China is still struggling to escape a cycle of deflation [38]. The verdict is stimulus-driven stabilisation in markets, with an unresolved balance-sheet problem underneath.

PMIs & Activity: The most recent official survey is February’s non-manufacturing PMI at 50.4 [37], which says services are holding. Activity indicators are positive at the margin. Express delivery posted fast growth in the first two months [39], and railway cargo volume rose in January and February [40]. Households are the soft spot. Food and beverage operators report slowing consumer spending [41], and Chinese lawmakers are targeting the job-market bias against workers over 35 [42]. Taken together, services and logistics hold while household demand and goods do the damage.

Credit Impulse: Credit is where the policy has to show up, and the evidence is still intent rather than loan growth. The central bank’s pledge of more tools [34] is the clearest signal, alongside a $7 billion state-backed fund that Bank of China set up to support technology development [43]. The bigger headline is a US$1 trillion reserves fund for Hong Kong, which Yahoo Finance describes as a secret plan [44]. Foreign money moved first: the IIF reports large February inflows into Chinese stocks and EM debt [45]. Until new loan figures show household borrowing turning up, the impulse is a bet on Beijing’s execution rather than on bank balance sheets.

Property: Property is where the stimulus story still runs into trouble. The developer plumbing is still under strain. China Evergrande and others were ordered to repay $1.8 billion of deposit pledges to a property unit [46], and some Hong Kong banks are refusing home loans for a Vanke project in Tai Po [47]. Official policy is pushing quality over volume, and SCMP’s analysts warn that the push for better homes adds stress for developers [48]. Some developers are less stretched: Country Garden’s unit forecast higher annual earnings [49].

Fiscal, Policy & Trade: Trade is the second drag. China’s tariffs on US agricultural products took effect [50], and AP reports Beijing is taking issue with tying tariffs to fentanyl [51]. US meat exporters are days away from being shut out of China [52]. Beijing is also watching US retailers, and Business Insider reads China’s warning to Walmart on tariffs as a sign it is worried about local businesses [53]. The Guardian’s argument is that China can live with Trump’s tariffs [54]. On the fiscal side, the 5% target leaves the mix open, and the state is promising consumption a larger role [55].

Markets & Flows: Chinese equities are doing the work. The Hang Seng closed at 23,959.98, up 2.12% in the latest session and 5.92% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). The Shanghai Composite is at 3,419.56 index points, up 2.18% over 20 sessions, and the CSI 300 ETF (ASHR) at 27.91 USD is up 4.73% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). FXI at 37.66 USD is up 10.25% over 20 sessions, and the internet ETF KWEB at 36.78 USD is up 7.11% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). The yuan is steady, with USD/CNY at 7.2371, down 0.71% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). Flows agree. Reuters headlines that Trump has made Chinese stocks “somewhat” great again [56], and Bloomberg reports Hong Kong’s stock market booming while Wall Street is in turmoil [57].

New / Most Important: The most useful signal is that the consumption push is now a written, numbered plan. The 30-point toolbox [33] turns a vague promise into a checklist, and that is the kind of signal equities tend to pay for. The test is whether it reaches household income, and developer stress is the counterweight [48]. The debate over where the 5% growth will come from is still open [35]. A plan that does not reach incomes is a financing exercise for the banks, not a demand story.

Playbook ✓: Own China exposure through the liquid large caps and the internet ETFs on pullbacks rather than chasing the 20-session move. Keep the yuan position light because USD/CNY is steady, and avoid developers and mainland property names until developer balance sheets stabilise. What changes the call: a consumption plan that shows up in household income data would extend the rally into consumer names, while a new US tariff tied to fentanyl [51] would hit the export names first. ⚠ Divergence: the Hang Seng is up 5.92% over 20 sessions while Evergrande and others were ordered to repay $1.8 billion of deposit pledges to a property unit [46], so the equity rally is pricing a policy the developer balance sheets have not yet confirmed.

Macro Stance: Japan is slowing into a rate-hike cycle, and that is the uncomfortable mix for equities. Reuters reports the fourth-quarter GDP was downgraded with US tariffs clouding the outlook [58], and CNBC says the revision complicates the BOJ’s rate outlook [59]. Tariffs are biting exporters: the trade minister failed to win an assurance on exemption from the 25% levies [60], as Fortune also reports [61]. Living costs are climbing, and Reuters says the service-sector mood is souring as a result [62]. The bond market has moved first: Bloomberg reports the 10-year yield at its highest since 2008 on bets for BOJ hikes [63]. Officials are talking about an end to deflation [64], and sources say a rate hike could be discussed in May [65].

Activity & Currency: The Nikkei 225 closed at 37,053.10, up 0.72% in the latest session but down 6.10% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). USD/JPY at 147.9490 is down 3.29% over 20 sessions, so the yen has strengthened into the rate story (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14), and Yahoo Finance flags stretched bull positioning in the yen [66]. Inside the index, SoftBank is down 17.55% over 20 sessions and Tokyo Electron 15.27%, while Advantest rose 5.30% in the latest session (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). Wages and borrowing tell two stories. Major companies agreed to sizeable pay rises [67], but consumers are leaning on credit, with mobile loans lifting borrowing to an 11-year high [68]. Bloomberg’s framing is that banks boom while shoppers scrimp a year after the rate pivot [69].

Playbook ✓: Underweight Japanese equities and trim the high-beta technology names, SoftBank and Tokyo Electron first, since they carry the most damage over 20 sessions. Fade the rate-sensitive bank trade that Bloomberg describes as booming [69], because consumer credit is the weak link. On the currency, the yen’s 20-session strength looks stretched, so take profit on short USD/JPY into any move back toward the 152.99 February reference (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). What changes the call is a clear pass-through from wage gains to consumer spending, or a US tariff exemption for Japan, which would lift the exporters.

Macro Stance: Australia is a Wall Street proxy in this sell-off, and the correlation is what fund managers are selling. Morgan Stanley is bearish on the ASX because of its correlation with Wall Street [70], and BlackRock has cut its exposure to Australian shares, citing poor value [71]. Trade policy is not helping. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese called US tariffs “not a friendly act” after Trump refused an exemption for Australia [72]. Canberra will not retaliate [73], which keeps the dispute contained but offers no offset. Super funds are feeling the reset, with AFR reporting that Trump’s economic reset is hitting major super fund returns [74]. The stance stays bearish until the correlation loosens or Washington changes its position on exemptions.

Demand & Financing: The ASX 200 closed at 7,789.70, down 8.95% over 20 sessions and up 0.52% in the latest session (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). The Commonwealth Bank is down 13.95% over 20 sessions, Fortescue is down 16.65% and BHP is down 5.55% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). AUD/USD at 0.6287 is down 0.47% over 20 sessions, so the currency is not cushioning the drop (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). Households are stretched. Australia’s housing market reached a record $11.032 trillion even as Sydney and Melbourne lost value [75], rental affordability in Sydney has hit a new low [76], and power prices for some are set to rise nearly 9 per cent from mid-year [77]. The growth engine is the data-centre build-out, with 175 new data centres and $26b of investment [78].

Playbook ✓: Stay underweight the ASX 200 and the big banks, and keep miners only where the China demand story is clean. Iron ore is split: Singapore prices rose on optimism about China demand [79], while accidents at the Simandou project have prompted an inquiry [80]. The trigger for a change is the Wall Street correlation. If US equities stabilise and the link loosens, the ASX can outperform. The other trigger is policy. An exemption for Australia from US tariffs would move the call to neutral, and that has not happened yet.

Macro Stance: Poland’s central bank is holding the line, and the zloty is the beneficiary. Governor Glapiński said there are no reasons to cut rates now [81], and wGospodarce’s headline on the NBP chief leaves no illusions about a rate cut, “Prezes NBP nie zostawia złudzeń na obniżkę stóp” [82]. The NBP projects inflation at 4.9% this year and the target only in 2027: “Inflacja wyniesie w tym roku 4,9%. Do celu dojdziemy dopiero w 2027” [83]. The governor also called the horizon to target “dość odległy”, quite distant, in TVN24’s words [84]. February’s price data surprised. Money.pl headlined “Zaskoczenie w lutym”, a surprise in February [85], and then explained that a change in the inflation basket weights pulled the figure lower [86]. The NBP says the GUS revision does not materially change its projection [87]. The message for investors is simple: rates stay high for longer.

Markets: The zloty is the strongest part of the story. USD/PLN is at 3.8502, down 3.33% over 20 sessions, and EUR/PLN at 4.1794 is up only 0.31% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). The iShares MSCI Poland ETF (EPOL) is at 28.50 USD, up 10.21% over 20 sessions, and the WIG20 total-return tracker is at 52.31 PLN, up 6.79% over 20 sessions and 2.65% in the latest session (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). The leaders are banks and energy. PKO Bank Polski is at 78.12 PLN, up 11.19% over 20 sessions, Bank Pekao at 184.05 PLN is up 6.79%, and mBank at 795.00 PLN is up 12.22% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). Orlen at 67.39 PLN is up 17.02% and PGE at 7.76 PLN is up 14.18% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). The laggard is CD Projekt, at 216.00 PLN and down 4.76% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). The early-March sell-off was a zloty story in its own right. Rzeczpospolita headlined a “Wyprzedaż złotego”, a sell-off of the zloty, on March 10 [88], which makes the 20-session recovery more convincing.

Fiscal & Politics: Fiscal and political risk is real, and the market is treating it as headline noise. Business Insider Polska reports that Fitch has issued a decision on Poland’s rating, “Agencja Fitch o ratingu kredytowym Polski. Jest decyzja” [89]. Defence is the fiscal priority. Poland has asked NATO to raise the minimum defence spending to 3% of GDP [90], and Tusk has announced military training for all men [91]. Politically the presidential race is tightening. Bloomberg reports a far-right candidate jumping to second place [92], and Le Monde says the far right is picking up steam as the election approaches [93]. Biejat, according to Bankier, says that as president she will sort out the mortgage market [94]. On the EU side, Credit Agricole’s chief economist says the Union is moving towards loosening fiscal rules [95].

Corporate & Sectors: Banks are carrying the index. Money.pl’s headline on the largest Polish bank reads “Największy bank w Polsce pochwalił się zyskiem. Skok o prawie 4 mld zł”, the biggest bank boasted a profit jump of almost PLN 4 billion [96]. Strefa Inwestorów asks whether PKO’s 2025 dividend could be record-setting [97], and PKO wants to close its Swiss franc saga in 2025 [98]. BNP Paribas’s Polish unit reported a 132% surge in full-year net profit [99]. E-commerce is the other growth story. Allegro sees earnings from Poland rising up to 12% in 2025 [100], Bankier headlines double-digit profit growth, “Allegro zakłada dwucyfrowy wzrost zysku” [101], and the company proposed a $364 mln buyback [102]. Dino Polska is looking for 1,300 workers [103], a sign of store expansion. Orlen still lacks a final deal with Sołowow on small nuclear [104]. Housing is the weak corner: apartment prices in Warsaw and Kraków fell year on year for the first time in three years [105].

Geopolitics & Security: Security is the bid under the defence names, and Washington is the risk. Bloomberg reports Trump is straining ties with Europe’s key US ally, Poland [106]. Poland’s president asked Washington to move nuclear warheads to Polish territory, according to the FT via Reuters [107], and Duda told the BBC that US nuclear weapons in Poland would be a deterrent for Russia [108]. Poland wants 100,000 volunteers for military training in 2027 [109]. US officials have said they will retaliate if Poland introduces a tax on big tech [110], so fiscal choices now carry trade risk. Prosecutors say Russia posed as a Belarusian refugee to set fire to a Warsaw mall [111], a reminder of the hostile backdrop.

New / Most Important: The signal that matters is the NBP’s path. Inflation at 4.9% this year and a target only in 2027 [83] keeps rates high for longer, which supports bank margins and the zloty. Glapiński’s “quite distant” horizon [84] is the answer investors were waiting for. The risk is a dovish turn arriving with the zloty already strong. Money.pl asks whether the NBP will intervene in the zloty and headlines the governor’s answer as an unambiguous declaration [112], which tells you the central bank is watching the currency closely.

Playbook ✓: Own the banks (PKO, Pekao and mBank) and PZU into the hold, keep Orlen and PGE as the energy-and-defence bridge, and avoid rate-sensitive developers while apartment prices fall year on year. The call changes if the NBP sounds dovish before the zloty stabilises, which would squeeze bank margins, or if the big-tech tax threat becomes a formal measure against Polish business, which would hit growth. ⚠ Divergence: the WIG20 total-return tracker is up 6.79% over 20 sessions while apartment prices in Warsaw and Kraków are falling for the first time in three years [105], so equities are running ahead of the housing data.

Narrative: Technology is the epicentre of the sell-off. XLK is at 213.94, up 3.02% in the latest session but down 10.55% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). The AI capex debate sets the tone. Oracle’s third-quarter call highlighted record backlog and cloud growth [113], which is the demand case, while Business Insider points out that Nvidia’s 30% sell-off has made the stock cheaper than when ChatGPT launched, on one metric [114]. Intel’s new chief executive gives the chip side a turnaround story that investors are willing to pay for [115].

Reported: Adobe beat its first-quarter estimates, but its revenue guidance disappointed and the stock fell 14% [116]. Stocktwits summed up the retail mood as hitting rock bottom [117]. Oracle is the other print in the window, and its call put the backlog at the centre of the story [113].

EPS Upside Watch: Oracle is the name set up for a surprise. Its backlog is the demand evidence, and the stock is 14.14% below its February reference (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). Adobe is the cautionary case: a beat did not stop the sell-off when the guide missed [118].

⚡ Breaking Convention: The convention says AI leaders are the place to hide from tariffs, yet the crowd is doing the opposite. Nvidia has overtaken Tesla as the most-held stock on Robinhood, fuelled by Gen Z interest [119], so retail is buying the AI drawdown rather than leaving it.

Narrative: Communication services are losing the consumer. XLC is at 96.58, up 1.83% in the latest session but down 7.73% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). Telecom is the weakest link: Verizon and AT&T slid after the giants signalled near-term softness amid competitive headwinds [120]. Disney’s shares sank under sagging consumer sentiment [121], which ties the sector to the same household squeeze that is hitting retail.

Reported: The reported theme is guidance rather than a clean beat or miss. Telecom leaders flagged softness [120], and Google is replacing its assistant with Gemini [122], a product shift rather than a reported number.

EPS Upside Watch: Alphabet is the name with room to surprise, given its push into small reactors [123] and its support, alongside Amazon, for tripling nuclear capacity by 2050 [124]. The set-up is thin across the rest of the sector, which is itself the signal for the next few weeks.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Streaming is supposed to be a mature, low-growth business, yet Netflix, Amazon and Peacock are going big on popular YouTubers [125]. The spend says the streaming war has moved into creator content, and the sector’s multiple has not caught up with that.

Narrative: Credit is the risk. XLF is at 48.52, down 6.15% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14), and Goldman Sachs says US credit spreads will get a lot wider amid tariffs [126]. Reuters reports spreads have already hit their widest in about six months on recession fears [127], and JPMorgan’s economist puts the US recession odds at 40% [10].

Reported: Bank of America is cutting 150 junior investment-banking jobs, sources say [128]. Goldman Sachs cut its S&P 500 year-end target to 6,200 as the economic outlook weighs on profit forecasts [129], a strategist’s call rather than a reported quarter.

EPS Upside Watch: SoFi’s $5 billion personal-loan agreement with Blue Owl [130] shows lending volume still moving, the best set-up for a surprise in the group. Goldman’s new option for downside protection [131] shows where client demand for volatility protection is heading.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The curve is the signal against the sell-off. The 10Y−2Y spread is +29 bps and widened by 8 bps over 20 observations (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-14). A steeper curve usually widens net interest margins, which argues the bank sell-off has run ahead of its earnings mechanics.

Narrative: Oil is the sector’s problem. WTI is at 67.18 USD and Brent at 70.58 USD, down 5.77% and 5.92% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). OPEC+ fuel exports hit a record and blunt the group’s crude supply cut [132], and Crude Oil Prices Today asks whether prices can stay above $60 as an oversupply spiral builds [133].

Reported: Shell’s shares rose while the market fell [134]. The news in energy is about deals and power rather than prints. Chevron is advancing plans to develop US data centres with its own power generation [135].

EPS Upside Watch: Nothing in the headlines screams upside for the group. The swing factor is sanctions, which could tighten supply quickly. China’s state firms are curbing Russian oil imports on sanctions risks [136], and Washington is ramping up sanctions on Russia’s oil, gas and banking sectors [137].

⚡ Breaking Convention: Iran sanctions are propping up oil prices [138], which cuts against the oversupply story. Energy is flat over 20 sessions, with XLE up 0.06%, even as crude fell 5.77% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). The divergence is the signal: equities are not paying for the crude sell-off.

Narrative: Industrials are split between tariff costs and power demand. XLI is at 131.13, down 4.90% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). The 25% steel and aluminium tariffs took effect [4], and US physical aluminium premiums hit a record on the duties [139].

Reported: Daimler Truck is cutting costs by $1.1 billion in Europe after an earnings slump [140]. Boeing’s problems continue. A US official says the company has lost Americans’ trust and needs strict oversight [141], and Reuters reports faulty parts on 787 jets slipped through in Italy [142].

EPS Upside Watch: GE Vernova’s new partnership [143] is the demand-side upside. Power equipment is the part of industrials most tied to the data-centre build-out, while the aerospace names carry the most scandal risk.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Boeing is up 4.95% over five sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14) even as the safety headlines pile up [142]. The market is looking past the scandal toward output, not reputation.

Narrative: Consumers are the weak link. XLY is at 196.70, up 2.13% in the latest session but down 13.39% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). Consumer sentiment fell to its lowest since 2022 on tariff worries [2], and Business Insider quotes Dollar General’s chief executive saying shoppers only have enough money for basic essentials [13]. Tesla, the group’s best-known retail name, is down 29.77% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14).

Reported: Ulta issued weak guidance, citing consumer uncertainty, rising competition and company missteps [144], and Dollar General said store closures dented its fourth quarter [145]. Hugo Boss warned of lingering uncertainty amid weak consumer sentiment [146].

EPS Upside Watch: Dollar General is the upside case. Its sales guidance came in above estimates [147], and shoppers trading down to low-cost options lift the discount channel [148]. The set-up favours value retail over the broad discretionary names.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Dollar General rose on guidance above estimates [147] while its chief executive says 2025 won’t be better [12]. The market is rewarding the discount channel for the same shoppers the CEO describes as cash-strapped.

Narrative: Staples are where the trade-down is paying. XLP is at 79.51, up 0.23% in the latest session but down 4.04% over five sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). Penny-pinching consumers are looking for low-cost options, and Dollar General and Dollar Tree shares rose on it [148]. Egg prices are a live policy story, with the Justice Department investigating major producers [149].
Reported: Henkel’s growth guidance disappointed as weak North America weighed on sales [150], which is the reported pressure in household goods.

The bulls are pricing a milestone, while the sceptics are pricing the distance between a milestone and a product. The Rigetti reference of 12.25 and the IonQ reference of 38.65 are the marks those names still sit below. No dated print for these names is in the headlines, so the trade has no fixed date. Issuance is the trigger to watch. Any new raise or at-the-market programme that lands in a rally tells you the company is taking the money the crowd is offering, as IonQ did [236]. The instrument risk is leverage. Defiance launched 2X leveraged ETFs on Rocket Lab and Hims & Hers [243], and leveraged wrappers are arriving on the names the crowd loves. Leverage doubles the exit problem in stocks that move this much in a session.

Why Retail Is Here: Retail investors treat Tesla as a loyalty stock, not a trade. Business Insider’s headline is that three retail investors explain why they are sticking with it after an $800 billion wipeout [244], and CNBC says retail investors can’t quit their love for Tesla [245]. The crowd’s story is about the founder. When Business Insider wrote that the stock had been cut in half and investors wanted their CEO back [246], it captured the emotional core, which is loyalty to a person rather than to a product. That makes the dip feel like a temporary discount on a company that will eventually be worth more.

Where It Breaks: Tesla closed at 249.98 USD, up 3.86% in the latest session, down 4.83% over five sessions and down 29.77% over 20 from a 355.94 reference (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). The observable break is a daily close below 249.98, the latest session’s level, which would fail the bounce. The instrument risk is the sales story. The Verge reports that Tesla registrations, and public opinion, are in free fall [247], and JPMorgan says the stock’s fall has no clear analogue [248]. A buyer who waits for the registrations to turn is buying the narrative, not the numbers.

Why Retail Is Here: Gold is the crowd’s safe haven, and the $3,000 level is the proof point. Bloomberg’s headline reads “Gold Breaks Through $3,000 as Trump Turbocharges Record Rally” [158], and Reuters reports that Trump-driven turbulence is drawing new investors into gold [249]. The retail logic is simple: when stocks correct and the dollar wobbles, buy the metal that needs no balance sheet. Bankier.pl’s “Doczekaliśmy się! Kurs złota sięgnął 3 000 dolarów za uncję”, roughly ‘at last, gold has reached $3,000 an ounce’ [250], shows the same euphoria in Polish.

Where It Breaks: Gold futures closed at 3,001.10 USD, up 0.33% in the latest session, 2.99% over five sessions and 1.89% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). The round level is $3,000 [158], and a close back under it would end the headline. The dated event is the Fed’s decision on Wednesday [9], and a firmer dollar is the risk, given that the dollar index is already down 3.35% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). For the ETF crowd, the instrument risk is the metal’s own price. SLV is up 4.24% over 20 sessions and GLD 1.82%, and a position bought on a headline carries the full drawdown if the dollar firms (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14).

Why Retail Is Here: The power bill for artificial intelligence is the story. Amazon and Google signed a pledge to support tripling nuclear capacity by 2050 [124], and CNBC reports Amazon, Google and Meta backing the same target [251]. Retail reads a pledge of that size as a ready customer for small reactors, and Alphabet is pushing small-reactor deployments to cut cost [123]. The crowd’s version is short. The AI build-out needs power that never stops, and nuclear is the clean option that does.

Where It Breaks: NuScale closed at 17.51 USD, up 15.12% in the latest session but down 29.14% over 20 sessions from a 24.71 reference (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). Oklo sits at 27.72 USD, down 49.63% over 20 sessions from 55.03. The observable break is a close back under the 17.51 level after the surge, and the cost story is the threat. Reuters reports small nuclear power is struggling at the cusp of the US electricity demand boom [252], and Stocktwits flagged that retail sentiment pulled back as NuScale and Oklo surged [192]. The instrument risk is liquidity: low-priced small caps where one headline moves the whole group.

geo.label: hold / data dependent
parts: Macro Stance

The S&P 500 closed at 5,638.94 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14), down 7.79% over 20 sessions even after a 2.13% bounce in the latest session. The index has slipped into correction, and CNN put it bluntly: “Dow slides and S&P 500 closes in correction as Trump’s trade war escalates” [[n12064]]. The pressure is coming through the household. Consumer sentiment fell to its lowest since 2022 on tariff worries [[n11595]], and inflation expectations jumped [[n11626]]. The 25% tariffs on steel and aluminum imports took effect and Europe retaliated [[n8899]]. The data cut the other way: February CPI eased to 2.8%, below forecasts [[n11417]], and the wholesale price measure was flat [[n11578]]. Washington removed one risk as well, with the spending bill signed and the shutdown averted [[n12255]] [[n12259]]. The Fed decides on Wednesday, and the pre-meeting framing is simply what to expect [[n12175]]. JPMorgan’s economist puts the odds of a US recession at 40% [[n0524]]. The data support holding risk while the tariff shock works through household budgets.
Rates & Curve

At the prior close the Treasury par curve had the 2Y at 4.02%, the 10Y at 4.31% and the 30Y at 4.62%, with the 10Y−2Y spread at +29 bps (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-14). Over 20 observations the 2Y fell 29 bps from 4.31% and the 10Y fell 21 bps from 4.52%, so the spread widened by 8 bps. The curve is positively sloped, and the 20-observation move is bull steepening (both down, 2Y down more) (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-14). The market is paying for earlier easing, not for a sharper cycle. Equities are pricing something else: the Nasdaq 100 is down 10.56% over 20 sessions, and the VIX, at 21.77, is up 44.17% over the same span (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). The dollar index sits at 103.72 index points, down 3.35% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14), and Bloomberg reports Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling the currency’s decline a natural adjustment [[n4008]]. Lower front-end yields with a softer dollar is the mix that rescues long-duration assets, but only if volatility stops rising.
New / Most Important

The signal that matters is what the household squeeze does to demand. Reuters reported consumer confidence sinking on tariff fears as inflation expectations jumped [[n11626]], and CNBC put March’s reading at its lowest since 2022 [[n11595]]. Retailers are saying the same thing. Dollar General’s chief executive warned that consumers are cash-strapped and that 2025 will not be better [[n3944]], and Business Insider quotes her saying shoppers only have enough money for ‘basic essentials’ [[n3942]]. The Fed is the other half of the trade. Bloomberg reports markets expect two cuts this year, starting in September [[n12174]], which is why the front end has rallied while equities fell. If the Wednesday decision keeps that path, the bond rally can carry. If it pushes back, the steepening stalls and the high-beta growth names that have been hit hardest face another leg down.
Playbook ✓

Stay at neutral equity exposure and rotate inside it rather than adding beta. Keep duration on through the Wednesday decision: the 2Y has already fallen 29 bps over 20 observations, and long Treasuries (TLT) are up 1.68% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14), so the market leans that way. Buy quality on down days rather than chasing the 2.13% bounce, and keep a volatility hedge while the VIX sits well above its February reference of 15.10 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). The call changes in two directions. A VIX close back under 15.10 with the 2Y still falling would make the rally broad and justify adding cyclicals. A 10Y yield back above its February level of 4.52%, with tariff escalation in the headlines, would argue for cutting duration and staying defensive.

geo.label: fiscal pivot / easing bias
parts: Macro Stance

Europe is the best-positioned large block for the coming weeks, and the reason is fiscal rather than monetary. Germany struck a historic debt deal and the euro rallied on it [[n3589]] [[n3588]]. The ECB has already cut its key rate to 2.5% on March 6 [[n3356]], and German inflation fell, which gives the ECB more room to ease further [[n3594]]. EUR/USD is at 1.0856, up 3.77% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). Reuters’ morning note framed the shift as “Europe, China shine as US exceptionalism fades” [[n3624]], and the New York Times reports that Trump’s moves are boosting stocks overseas [[n3628]]. The caveat is that the rally is in the home market, not in US listings, since the FT notes that US listings often fail to lift European valuations [[n3629]].
Credit & Inflation

Inflation risk is two-sided. Lagarde warned that trade and defence shocks could amplify euro zone inflation [[n3527]], and that higher defence spending could push prices up [[n3518]]. The ECB wage tracker still points to easing negotiated wages [[n3521]], which keeps the disinflation path intact. Growth is weaker at the edges: the UK economy shrank unexpectedly in January [[n3610]], and France’s borrowing costs are near a 14-year high before a Fitch review [[n3551]]. The Bundesbank chief warned that US tariffs could extend Germany’s recession [[n3576]], which is why the German package matters for the whole bloc. The market shows the split: the DAX is at 22,986.82, up 2.10% over 20 sessions, while the STOXX 600 is at 546.60, down 1.05% over the same span (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14).
New / Most Important

The signal that matters is the German fiscal turn, and its beneficiaries are wider than defence. Euronews framed it as “Beyond defence: Stocks set to gain from Germany’s economic revolution” [[n3540]], and DIW says the fiscal expansion would boost German GDP from 2026 [[n3596]]. EU ministers have also backed a proposal for a temporary exemption on defence spending in EU rules [[n3462]]. Defence is the headline. Construction, industrial capex and utilities are the quieter channel the fiscal plan reaches.
Playbook ✓

Buy German and broad euro-area cyclicals on pullbacks, keep a defence sleeve as the hedge, and avoid the autos that tariff headlines are hitting. A euro long against the dollar makes sense now that the US shutdown risk has passed [[n12259]]. The call changes in two ways. A fresh US tariff escalation on EU goods, such as the 200% tariff threat on EU alcohol [[n12126]], would move the block to neutral. An ECB pause read as a tightening bias would do the same, although the cut to 2.5% makes that unlikely in the near term.

geo.label: stimulus promised / property still falling
parts: Macro Stance

Beijing is talking about demand, and equity markets are listening. Beijing has said it will “vigorously boost consumption” [[n1541]], and the plan arrives as a 30-point toolbox [[n1546]]. The central bank said it will create “more tools” to shore up the economy [[n1481]]. The 5% growth target leaves most of the work to policy [[n1256]], and Fortune argues China has only one real way to hit it [[n1220]]. The official data are mixed rather than weak. The non-manufacturing PMI was 50.4 in February [[n0827]], but Bloomberg’s headline says China is still struggling to escape a cycle of deflation [[n1374]]. The verdict is stimulus-driven stabilisation in markets, with an unresolved balance-sheet problem underneath.
PMIs & Activity

The most recent official survey is February’s non-manufacturing PMI at 50.4 [[n0827]], which says services are holding. Activity indicators are positive at the margin. Express delivery posted fast growth in the first two months [[n1523]], and railway cargo volume rose in January and February [[n1311]]. Households are the soft spot. Food and beverage operators report slowing consumer spending [[n1480]], and Chinese lawmakers are targeting the job-market bias against workers over 35 [[n1429]]. Taken together, services and logistics hold while household demand and goods do the damage.
Credit Impulse

Credit is where the policy has to show up, and the evidence is still intent rather than loan growth. The central bank’s pledge of more tools [[n1481]] is the clearest signal, alongside a $7 billion state-backed fund that Bank of China set up to support technology development [[n1471]]. The bigger headline is a US$1 trillion reserves fund for Hong Kong, which Yahoo Finance describes as a secret plan [[n1527]]. Foreign money moved first: the IIF reports large February inflows into Chinese stocks and EM debt [[n1406]]. Until new loan figures show household borrowing turning up, the impulse is a bet on Beijing’s execution rather than on bank balance sheets.
Property

Property is where the stimulus story still runs into trouble. The developer plumbing is still under strain. China Evergrande and others were ordered to repay $1.8 billion of deposit pledges to a property unit [[n1213]], and some Hong Kong banks are refusing home loans for a Vanke project in Tai Po [[n1267]]. Official policy is pushing quality over volume, and SCMP’s analysts warn that the push for better homes adds stress for developers [[n1319]]. Some developers are less stretched: Country Garden’s unit forecast higher annual earnings [[n1503]].
Fiscal, Policy & Trade

Trade is the second drag. China’s tariffs on US agricultural products took effect [[n1315]], and AP reports Beijing is taking issue with tying tariffs to fentanyl [[n1392]]. US meat exporters are days away from being shut out of China [[n1511]]. Beijing is also watching US retailers, and Business Insider reads China’s warning to Walmart on tariffs as a sign it is worried about local businesses [[n1397]]. The Guardian’s argument is that China can live with Trump’s tariffs [[n1305]]. On the fiscal side, the 5% target leaves the mix open, and the state is promising consumption a larger role [[n1324]].
Markets & Flows

Chinese equities are doing the work. The Hang Seng closed at 23,959.98, up 2.12% in the latest session and 5.92% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). The Shanghai Composite is at 3,419.56 index points, up 2.18% over 20 sessions, and the CSI 300 ETF (ASHR) at 27.91 USD is up 4.73% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). FXI at 37.66 USD is up 10.25% over 20 sessions, and the internet ETF KWEB at 36.78 USD is up 7.11% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). The yuan is steady, with USD/CNY at 7.2371, down 0.71% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). Flows agree. Reuters headlines that Trump has made Chinese stocks “somewhat” great again [[n1488]], and Bloomberg reports Hong Kong’s stock market booming while Wall Street is in turmoil [[n1421]].
New / Most Important

The most useful signal is that the consumption push is now a written, numbered plan. The 30-point toolbox [[n1546]] turns a vague promise into a checklist, and that is the kind of signal equities tend to pay for. The test is whether it reaches household income, and developer stress is the counterweight [[n1319]]. The debate over where the 5% growth will come from is still open [[n1256]]. A plan that does not reach incomes is a financing exercise for the banks, not a demand story.
Playbook ✓

Own China exposure through the liquid large caps and the internet ETFs on pullbacks rather than chasing the 20-session move. Keep the yuan position light because USD/CNY is steady, and avoid developers and mainland property names until developer balance sheets stabilise. What changes the call: a consumption plan that shows up in household income data would extend the rally into consumer names, while a new US tariff tied to fentanyl [[n1392]] would hit the export names first. ⚠ Divergence: the Hang Seng is up 5.92% over 20 sessions while Evergrande and others were ordered to repay $1.8 billion of deposit pledges to a property unit [[n1213]], so the equity rally is pricing a policy the developer balance sheets have not yet confirmed.

geo.label: tariff drag / tightening bias
parts: Macro Stance

Japan is slowing into a rate-hike cycle, and that is the uncomfortable mix for equities. Reuters reports the fourth-quarter GDP was downgraded with US tariffs clouding the outlook [[n5388]], and CNBC says the revision complicates the BOJ’s rate outlook [[n2707]]. Tariffs are biting exporters: the trade minister failed to win an assurance on exemption from the 25% levies [[n5392]], as Fortune also reports [[n5443]]. Living costs are climbing, and Reuters says the service-sector mood is souring as a result [[n5391]]. The bond market has moved first: Bloomberg reports the 10-year yield at its highest since 2008 on bets for BOJ hikes [[n5385]]. Officials are talking about an end to deflation [[n5346]], and sources say a rate hike could be discussed in May [[n5345]].
Activity & Currency

The Nikkei 225 closed at 37,053.10, up 0.72% in the latest session but down 6.10% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). USD/JPY at 147.9490 is down 3.29% over 20 sessions, so the yen has strengthened into the rate story (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14), and Yahoo Finance flags stretched bull positioning in the yen [[n5427]]. Inside the index, SoftBank is down 17.55% over 20 sessions and Tokyo Electron 15.27%, while Advantest rose 5.30% in the latest session (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). Wages and borrowing tell two stories. Major companies agreed to sizeable pay rises [[n5488]], but consumers are leaning on credit, with mobile loans lifting borrowing to an 11-year high [[n5492]]. Bloomberg’s framing is that banks boom while shoppers scrimp a year after the rate pivot [[n5555]].
Playbook ✓

Underweight Japanese equities and trim the high-beta technology names, SoftBank and Tokyo Electron first, since they carry the most damage over 20 sessions. Fade the rate-sensitive bank trade that Bloomberg describes as booming [[n5555]], because consumer credit is the weak link. On the currency, the yen’s 20-session strength looks stretched, so take profit on short USD/JPY into any move back toward the 152.99 February reference (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). What changes the call is a clear pass-through from wage gains to consumer spending, or a US tariff exemption for Japan, which would lift the exporters.

geo.label: tariff spillover / US-beta drag
parts: Macro Stance

Australia is a Wall Street proxy in this sell-off, and the correlation is what fund managers are selling. Morgan Stanley is bearish on the ASX because of its correlation with Wall Street [[n0441]], and BlackRock has cut its exposure to Australian shares, citing poor value [[n0229]]. Trade policy is not helping. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese called US tariffs “not a friendly act” after Trump refused an exemption for Australia [[n0300]]. Canberra will not retaliate [[n11951]], which keeps the dispute contained but offers no offset. Super funds are feeling the reset, with AFR reporting that Trump’s economic reset is hitting major super fund returns [[n0284]]. The stance stays bearish until the correlation loosens or Washington changes its position on exemptions.
Demand & Financing

The ASX 200 closed at 7,789.70, down 8.95% over 20 sessions and up 0.52% in the latest session (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). The Commonwealth Bank is down 13.95% over 20 sessions, Fortescue is down 16.65% and BHP is down 5.55% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). AUD/USD at 0.6287 is down 0.47% over 20 sessions, so the currency is not cushioning the drop (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). Households are stretched. Australia’s housing market reached a record $11.032 trillion even as Sydney and Melbourne lost value [[n0367]], rental affordability in Sydney has hit a new low [[n0255]], and power prices for some are set to rise nearly 9 per cent from mid-year [[n0393]]. The growth engine is the data-centre build-out, with 175 new data centres and $26b of investment [[n0405]].
Playbook ✓

Stay underweight the ASX 200 and the big banks, and keep miners only where the China demand story is clean. Iron ore is split: Singapore prices rose on optimism about China demand [[n0345]], while accidents at the Simandou project have prompted an inquiry [[n0385]]. The trigger for a change is the Wall Street correlation. If US equities stabilise and the link loosens, the ASX can outperform. The other trigger is policy. An exemption for Australia from US tariffs would move the call to neutral, and that has not happened yet.

geo.label: hawkish hold / bank and defence bid
parts: Macro Stance

Poland’s central bank is holding the line, and the zloty is the beneficiary. Governor Glapiński said there are no reasons to cut rates now [[n3563]], and wGospodarce’s headline on the NBP chief leaves no illusions about a rate cut, “Prezes NBP nie zostawia złudzeń na obniżkę stóp” [[n6204]]. The NBP projects inflation at 4.9% this year and the target only in 2027: “Inflacja wyniesie w tym roku 4,9%. Do celu dojdziemy dopiero w 2027” [[n6233]]. The governor also called the horizon to target “dość odległy”, quite distant, in TVN24’s words [[n6177]]. February’s price data surprised. Money.pl headlined “Zaskoczenie w lutym”, a surprise in February [[n6253]], and then explained that a change in the inflation basket weights pulled the figure lower [[n6229]]. The NBP says the GUS revision does not materially change its projection [[n6239]]. The message for investors is simple: rates stay high for longer.
Markets

The zloty is the strongest part of the story. USD/PLN is at 3.8502, down 3.33% over 20 sessions, and EUR/PLN at 4.1794 is up only 0.31% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). The iShares MSCI Poland ETF (EPOL) is at 28.50 USD, up 10.21% over 20 sessions, and the WIG20 total-return tracker is at 52.31 PLN, up 6.79% over 20 sessions and 2.65% in the latest session (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). The leaders are banks and energy. PKO Bank Polski is at 78.12 PLN, up 11.19% over 20 sessions, Bank Pekao at 184.05 PLN is up 6.79%, and mBank at 795.00 PLN is up 12.22% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). Orlen at 67.39 PLN is up 17.02% and PGE at 7.76 PLN is up 14.18% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). The laggard is CD Projekt, at 216.00 PLN and down 4.76% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). The early-March sell-off was a zloty story in its own right. Rzeczpospolita headlined a “Wyprzedaż złotego”, a sell-off of the zloty, on March 10 [[n6015]], which makes the 20-session recovery more convincing.
Fiscal & Politics

Fiscal and political risk is real, and the market is treating it as headline noise. Business Insider Polska reports that Fitch has issued a decision on Poland’s rating, “Agencja Fitch o ratingu kredytowym Polski. Jest decyzja” [[n6255]]. Defence is the fiscal priority. Poland has asked NATO to raise the minimum defence spending to 3% of GDP [[n5601]], and Tusk has announced military training for all men [[n5600]]. Politically the presidential race is tightening. Bloomberg reports a far-right candidate jumping to second place [[n5605]], and Le Monde says the far right is picking up steam as the election approaches [[n5698]]. Biejat, according to Bankier, says that as president she will sort out the mortgage market [[n5947]]. On the EU side, Credit Agricole’s chief economist says the Union is moving towards loosening fiscal rules [[n6053]].
Corporate & Sectors

Banks are carrying the index. Money.pl’s headline on the largest Polish bank reads “Największy bank w Polsce pochwalił się zyskiem. Skok o prawie 4 mld zł”, the biggest bank boasted a profit jump of almost PLN 4 billion [[n6188]]. Strefa Inwestorów asks whether PKO’s 2025 dividend could be record-setting [[n6176]], and PKO wants to close its Swiss franc saga in 2025 [[n5678]]. BNP Paribas’s Polish unit reported a 132% surge in full-year net profit [[n5669]]. E-commerce is the other growth story. Allegro sees earnings from Poland rising up to 12% in 2025 [[n5671]], Bankier headlines double-digit profit growth, “Allegro zakłada dwucyfrowy wzrost zysku” [[n6163]], and the company proposed a $364 mln buyback [[n5672]]. Dino Polska is looking for 1,300 workers [[n6173]], a sign of store expansion. Orlen still lacks a final deal with Sołowow on small nuclear [[n6192]]. Housing is the weak corner: apartment prices in Warsaw and Kraków fell year on year for the first time in three years [[n6042]].
Geopolitics & Security

Security is the bid under the defence names, and Washington is the risk. Bloomberg reports Trump is straining ties with Europe’s key US ally, Poland [[n5693]]. Poland’s president asked Washington to move nuclear warheads to Polish territory, according to the FT via Reuters [[n5680]], and Duda told the BBC that US nuclear weapons in Poland would be a deterrent for Russia [[n5667]]. Poland wants 100,000 volunteers for military training in 2027 [[n5636]]. US officials have said they will retaliate if Poland introduces a tax on big tech [[n5618]], so fiscal choices now carry trade risk. Prosecutors say Russia posed as a Belarusian refugee to set fire to a Warsaw mall [[n5660]], a reminder of the hostile backdrop.
New / Most Important

The signal that matters is the NBP’s path. Inflation at 4.9% this year and a target only in 2027 [[n6233]] keeps rates high for longer, which supports bank margins and the zloty. Glapiński’s “quite distant” horizon [[n6177]] is the answer investors were waiting for. The risk is a dovish turn arriving with the zloty already strong. Money.pl asks whether the NBP will intervene in the zloty and headlines the governor’s answer as an unambiguous declaration [[n6169]], which tells you the central bank is watching the currency closely.
Playbook ✓

Own the banks (PKO, Pekao and mBank) and PZU into the hold, keep Orlen and PGE as the energy-and-defence bridge, and avoid rate-sensitive developers while apartment prices fall year on year. The call changes if the NBP sounds dovish before the zloty stabilises, which would squeeze bank margins, or if the big-tech tax threat becomes a formal measure against Polish business, which would hit growth. ⚠ Divergence: the WIG20 total-return tracker is up 6.79% over 20 sessions while apartment prices in Warsaw and Kraków are falling for the first time in three years [[n6042]], so equities are running ahead of the housing data.
Narrative

Technology is the epicentre of the sell-off. XLK is at 213.94, up 3.02% in the latest session but down 10.55% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). The AI capex debate sets the tone. Oracle’s third-quarter call highlighted record backlog and cloud growth [[n0507]], which is the demand case, while Business Insider points out that Nvidia’s 30% sell-off has made the stock cheaper than when ChatGPT launched, on one metric [[n6347]]. Intel’s new chief executive gives the chip side a turnaround story that investors are willing to pay for [[n3098]].
Reported

Adobe beat its first-quarter estimates, but its revenue guidance disappointed and the stock fell 14% [[n3005]]. Stocktwits summed up the retail mood as hitting rock bottom [[n3003]]. Oracle is the other print in the window, and its call put the backlog at the centre of the story [[n0507]].
EPS Upside Watch

Oracle is the name set up for a surprise. Its backlog is the demand evidence, and the stock is 14.14% below its February reference (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). Adobe is the cautionary case: a beat did not stop the sell-off when the guide missed [[n3002]].
⚡ Breaking Convention

The convention says AI leaders are the place to hide from tariffs, yet the crowd is doing the opposite. Nvidia has overtaken Tesla as the most-held stock on Robinhood, fuelled by Gen Z interest [[n6732]], so retail is buying the AI drawdown rather than leaving it.
Narrative

Communication services are losing the consumer. XLC is at 96.58, up 1.83% in the latest session but down 7.73% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). Telecom is the weakest link: Verizon and AT&T slid after the giants signalled near-term softness amid competitive headwinds [[n6517]]. Disney’s shares sank under sagging consumer sentiment [[n11287]], which ties the sector to the same household squeeze that is hitting retail.
Reported

The reported theme is guidance rather than a clean beat or miss. Telecom leaders flagged softness [[n6517]], and Google is replacing its assistant with Gemini [[n9661]], a product shift rather than a reported number.
EPS Upside Watch

Alphabet is the name with room to surprise, given its push into small reactors [[n6297]] and its support, alongside Amazon, for tripling nuclear capacity by 2050 [[n9554]]. The set-up is thin across the rest of the sector, which is itself the signal for the next few weeks.
⚡ Breaking Convention

Streaming is supposed to be a mature, low-growth business, yet Netflix, Amazon and Peacock are going big on popular YouTubers [[n9640]]. The spend says the streaming war has moved into creator content, and the sector’s multiple has not caught up with that.
Narrative

Credit is the risk. XLF is at 48.52, down 6.15% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14), and Goldman Sachs says US credit spreads will get a lot wider amid tariffs [[n3860]]. Reuters reports spreads have already hit their widest in about six months on recession fears [[n3899]], and JPMorgan’s economist puts the US recession odds at 40% [[n0524]].
Reported

Bank of America is cutting 150 junior investment-banking jobs, sources say [[n11376]]. Goldman Sachs cut its S&P 500 year-end target to 6,200 as the economic outlook weighs on profit forecasts [[n2923]], a strategist’s call rather than a reported quarter.
EPS Upside Watch

SoFi’s $5 billion personal-loan agreement with Blue Owl [[n6687]] shows lending volume still moving, the best set-up for a surprise in the group. Goldman’s new option for downside protection [[n6777]] shows where client demand for volatility protection is heading.
⚡ Breaking Convention

The curve is the signal against the sell-off. The 10Y−2Y spread is +29 bps and widened by 8 bps over 20 observations (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-14). A steeper curve usually widens net interest margins, which argues the bank sell-off has run ahead of its earnings mechanics.
Narrative

Oil is the sector’s problem. WTI is at 67.18 USD and Brent at 70.58 USD, down 5.77% and 5.92% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). OPEC+ fuel exports hit a record and blunt the group’s crude supply cut [[n9373]], and Crude Oil Prices Today asks whether prices can stay above $60 as an oversupply spiral builds [[n9974]].
Reported

Shell’s shares rose while the market fell [[n3078]]. The news in energy is about deals and power rather than prints. Chevron is advancing plans to develop US data centres with its own power generation [[n9601]].
EPS Upside Watch

Nothing in the headlines screams upside for the group. The swing factor is sanctions, which could tighten supply quickly. China’s state firms are curbing Russian oil imports on sanctions risks [[n3037]], and Washington is ramping up sanctions on Russia’s oil, gas and banking sectors [[n5014]].
⚡ Breaking Convention

Iran sanctions are propping up oil prices [[n9683]], which cuts against the oversupply story. Energy is flat over 20 sessions, with XLE up 0.06%, even as crude fell 5.77% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). The divergence is the signal: equities are not paying for the crude sell-off.

Industrials are split between tariff costs and power demand. XLI is at 131.13, down 4.90% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). The 25% steel and aluminium tariffs took effect [[n8899]], and US physical aluminium premiums hit a record on the duties [[n12129]].
Reported

EPS Upside Watch

GE Vernova’s new partnership [[n6441]] is the demand-side upside. Power equipment is the part of industrials most tied to the data-centre build-out, while the aerospace names carry the most scandal risk.

earnings_pattern.title: Earnings Pattern — The Guidance Line Decides the Reaction
parts: Rewarded

Raised or better-than-expected guidance was rewarded. DocuSign surged 14% on strong earnings and an AI boost [[n3152]]. Dollar General rose when its sales guidance came in above estimates [[n3028]], even as it closed almost 100 stores in the fourth quarter [[n3131]] and said it would close 141 stores [[n4034]]. Allegro’s shares rose strongly as it announced a large buyback alongside good results [[n6189]], having proposed a $364 mln buyback [[n5672]]. Mercedes-Benz posted full-year EPS that beat expectations [[n3062]].
Punished

Beats with soft guidance were punished. Adobe fell 14% despite a better-than-expected quarter, as concerns about AI growth overshadowed the beat [[n3005]], and Stocktwits says disappointing revenue guidance overshadowed the first-quarter beat [[n3003]]. Ulta issued weak guidance, citing consumer uncertainty and rising competition [[n3095]]. BMW reported a 37% drop in annual net profit [[n3118]], and a 1 billion euro tariff hit [[n3115]] is coming on top. Daimler Truck is cutting $1.1 billion of costs after an earnings slump [[n3127]]. ContextLogic slipped after a fourth-quarter miss [[n3023]], and CATL posted its slowest profit growth in six years [[n3121]].
Pattern

Across the two weeks the guidance line did more work than the quarter. Companies that beat and raised were rewarded. Companies that beat but guided soft were punished, most visibly Adobe, where a clean beat ended in a 14% drop. Consumer names carry the most guidance risk, with Hugo Boss warning of lingering uncertainty amid weak consumer sentiment [[n11516]]. The sharpest exception is discount retail. Dollar General reported record sales in the quarter [[n0539]] and guided above estimates, showing that trade-down traffic can be rewarded even while the chief executive warns that shoppers are cash-strapped [[n3944]].
Attention into EPS

The next scheduled print in the headlines is Nio’s fourth-quarter report on March 21 [[n2837]], and the stock is up 15.02% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14), so the bar has moved before the number. Software names such as Adobe will be judged on forward numbers rather than the quarter. Chinese EV makers are being told to show resilience despite tariffs [[n3192]].
Playbook

Buy into beats that raise the forward numbers, as Dollar General and DocuSign did, and do not chase beats that guide soft, as Adobe did. Into the Nio print, size small and hedge with the sector. The risk is a soft guide after a 15% run.

Treat the crypto complex as high-beta, not as a hedge. flows.title: Capital Flows & Liquidity — Rates Carry the Trade, Credit Starts to Price Risk
parts: Global Liquidity

Liquidity is being added at the margin in Europe and China and withdrawn in Japan. The ECB cut its key rate to 2.5% on March 6 [[n3356]], and the Bank of England is set to keep rates on hold as global uncertainty mounts [[n3620]]. China’s central bank promised more tools [[n1481]], and a secret plan for a US$1 trillion reserves fund in Hong Kong has surfaced [[n1527]]. The Bank of Japan is the tightening outlier. Reuters reports it will scrutinise how higher rates hit banks and deposits [[n5424]], and the 10-year JGB yield has hit its highest since 2008 on bets for hikes [[n5385]]. Bitcoin is being read through the same lens. TradingView argues that global M2 is tightening its grip on the coin [[n2006]], and the Bank of Korea ruled it out of reserves [[n2040]].
Rates & Dollar

The curve is doing what a cutting market does. The 2Y is at 4.02% and the 10Y at 4.31% (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-14), with the 2Y down 29 bps over 20 observations. Europe is moving the same way: German inflation fell, which the market reads as room for the ECB to ease further [[n3594]]. The dollar is the swing factor. The dollar index is at 103.72 index points, down 3.35% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14), and Reuters reported on March 13 that the dollar rose as markets consolidated positions, with the outlook still downbeat [[n3575]]. The WSJ asks whether Trump’s new world order tests the dollar [[n12258]]. In credit, HYG is at 78.88 USD, down 0.99% over 20 sessions, and LQD at 107.95 USD is up 0.35% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14), while TLT is up 1.68% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14).
Credit Check

Credit is where a correction can turn into something worse. Reuters reports US corporate bond spreads hit their widest in about six months on recession fears [[n3899]], and Goldman Sachs says US credit spreads will get a lot wider amid tariffs [[n3860]]. High yield is holding up better than equities. HYG is down 0.99% over 20 sessions against a 7.79% drop for the S&P 500 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14), which says the bond market is pricing a slowdown rather than a default wave. France is the European warning sign, with borrowing costs near a 14-year high before a Fitch review [[n3551]]. Banks are feeling it first. A Motley Fool headline says the Monday sell-off hit Citigroup, Goldman Sachs and SoFi hardest [[n6302]].
Equity & Fund Flows

The flow data show the crowd still buying the dip while institutions cut. Reuters reports that investors bought the Magnificent 7 ETF amid the downturn [[n6559]], but Yahoo Finance says hedge funds cut their stakes in all of the Magnificent 7 stocks last quarter except one [[n4094]]. Reuters also reports that hedge funds sped up de-risking and likely have more to come [[n3862]], while Asian hedge funds outperformed their US peers as markets sold off [[n3929]]. Insiders are selling. Tech and banking insiders cashed in more than $800 million of stock, per Fortune [[n6491]]. Options show the hedging, with Moomoo reporting record put-options volume and asking whether a rebound is coming [[n12003]]. On buybacks, Allegro proposed a $364 mln buyback [[n5672]] and AIA unveiled a $1.6 billion buyback [[n1420]]. Large February inflows went into Chinese stocks and EM debt, per the IIF [[n1406]], and China sees record gold ETF inflows in February [[n4029]].
Portfolio Implication

Add duration on dips, keep credit in quality while the spread widening is still in play, and let the weaker dollar do the work for gold and Asian equities. Liquidity supports Europe and China at the margin and argues against crowding into Japan’s rate-sensitive banks. Bloomberg’s headline that banks boom while shoppers scrimp is the trade to fade rather than chase [[n5555]]. What would change the view is a sharp widening in high-yield spreads, which would say the bond market has moved from a growth scare to a default cycle, or a clear dollar rebound that lifts the funding costs of Asian carry trades.

anticipatory.title: The Fed’s Wednesday decision
parts: What Is Priced

Markets price the Fed to cut twice this year, starting in September [[n12174]], and the 2Y has already fallen 29 bps over 20 observations (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-14). The VIX at 21.77 has already jumped 44.17% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14). A hawkish surprise would push it higher and turn the correction into a broader drawdown. A firmer dollar from 103.72 index points would weigh on gold.

anticipatory.title: A Trump–Putin call and a Ukraine ceasefire
parts: What Is Priced

Trump and Putin are expected to speak as the US pushes for a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire [[n5106]], and the US has hinted at Ukraine concessions ahead of the call [[n5110]]. Putin has set out conditions for a ceasefire [[n5018]], and Russia and Ukraine traded overnight aerial attacks amid the proposed ceasefire talks [[n5071]] [[n5072]].
Conditional Expression

A ceasefire framework would be bearish for Rheinmetall, which is up 67.56% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14), and for the defence bid that has driven it. It would be bullish for autos and for Europe’s broad market, which has the most to gain from lower energy and tariff risk. A collapse of the talks does the reverse. It extends the defence trade and keeps oil’s geopolitical premium alive.
Risk

The talks are the risk. Putin’s conditions mean a deal could be a headline rather than a settlement [[n4805]], and the US strikes on the Houthis, which killed at least 31 people, show the region is still active [[n5109]].

anticipatory.title: Tariffs: talks or escalation
parts: What Is Priced

Canada and US officials are due to talk tariffs again, per CTV [[n4905]], and the EU has said it will impose counter tariffs on $28 billion of US goods [[n11965]]. The reciprocal tariff plan remains the framework behind the new duties [[n10197]], and the US is weighing a 25% tariff on copper imports [[n8902]].
Conditional Expression

A negotiated exemption for allies would relieve autos, industrials and metals, and it would support the bank and credit story. Escalation with counter-tariffs widens credit spreads, which Goldman sees getting much wider [[n3860]], and it hits European autos first.
Risk

Retaliation is already under way. Canada is set to impose 25% reciprocal tariffs after the US steel and aluminium duties [[n8409]], and Trump has threatened a 200% tariff on EU alcohol [[n12126]]. Each step widens the set of goods exposed, and aluminium premiums are already at a record on the duties [[n12129]].

anticipatory.title: China’s consumption plan: policy or property
parts: What Is Priced

Beijing has unveiled a 30-point toolbox to boost consumption [[n1546]], and the central bank has promised more tools [[n1481]]. Equities have priced part of the policy already: the Hang Seng is up 5.92% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-14).
Conditional Expression

If household income data follow the plan, the rally can extend into consumer names and the internet platforms. If developer stress keeps building [[n1319]], the policy looks like a financing exercise, and China ETFs are vulnerable to a reversal. The equity bid already assumes the plan reaches households, so a miss would be priced quickly.
Risk

Developer balance sheets are the tail. China Evergrande and others were ordered to repay $1.8 billion of deposit pledges [[n1213]], and SCMP’s analysts warn the push for better homes adds further developer stress [[n1319]]. A US tariff escalation tied to fentanyl [[n1392]] is the external shock.
